The ASV supplies *the* before an anarthrous second conjunct, so it is a rule 7 helper on the noun (rule 51); rule 11 keeps the italics from making it added. tou is already emptied by rule 20, hemon being free and taking *our*, so rule 76 does not free it to take a determiner in the other conjunct: PHP.1.19 and PHP.3.10 both put a second conjunct's supplied determiner on its noun, and no corpus article realizes a determiner outside its own conjunct. The margin's *our God and Saviour* would leave the noun bare, but the ASV's text is what is aligned.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV text reads 'Simon Peter' (Simon = Sigma-iota-mu-omega-nu), and the mapped textual_variant note relegates the other reading to the margin: 'Many ancient authorities read Symeon.' The note marks Symeon as what the ASV did not print, so the text renders r01.

Passive auxiliary is a helper on the lexical verb under rules 9 and 17.

Rule 23: the ASV gives the noun no determiner, so the article has no English realization, and under rule 21 the case preposition *of* stays with the noun. Not rule 23's article-before-a-name arm, which rule 57 confines to an article whose head noun is itself the name.
Source noun rendered of + noun heads on the noun under rule 17.

Rule 17: substantival adjective expanded with the generic *things*, headed on *all*.

Rule 31: a substantival article whose modifier is a prepositional phrase keeps the supplied relativizer and nothing else; πάντα has already taken the nominal *all things*. A reading giving the article *that pertain* whole is defensible.
Rules 31 and 62: the supplied lexical verb rides with the preposition of the prepositional predicate, headed on the word realizing the preposition.
Rule 19.
Rule 32: the substantival article supplies the pronoun only, the case preposition *of* riding along under rule 21.
Rule 32: the participle carries the relativizer, headed on the verb.
Rule 47: anarthrous ἴδιος carries the supplied possessive itself.

Rule 21: with no article present the dative case preposition *by* stays with the noun, discontinuously under rule 15. The corpus is unanimous for an anarthrous adjective plus noun (54/54), including idios itself at EPH.5.22, TIT.2.5, TIT.2.9 and EPH.4.28.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV text reads 'called us by his own glory and virtue': the possessive 'his own' renders the adjective idia with the datives, i.e. the base reading. The mapped textual_variant note puts the rival in the margin ('Some ancient authorities read through glory and virtue' = dia doxes kai aretes), confirming the base is the printed text.

alignments.note: Rule 35: preposition and relative fused into one English word; -by realizes the preposition, where- the pronoun.
Rule 9: supplied subject and auxiliary ride with the inflected verb, headed on the lexical verb.
Case preposition rides with the dative pronoun (rules 21, 36).
Rule 20 second arm: no other source word is present to take the supplied possessive, so the article is what 'his' realizes.
Superlative rendered by intensifier plus adjective; head on the lexical adjective (rule 17).
Rule 40: the conjunction is realized by the word introducing its English clause.
Rule 9: subject and modal auxiliary ride with the verb, headed on the lexical verb.
Rule 58: adjective and noun both anarthrous, so the supplied determiner and the case preposition go with the noun, discontinuously under rule 15.

Rule 31: the article precedes the noun it governs across the interposed prepositional phrase, so it takes the discontinuous 'the ... that' headed on 'the', with the case preposition riding along under rule 21.
The noun stands bare, its determiner having gone to the preceding article.
Rules 31 and 53: a prepositional phrase has no verb to carry the supplied copula, so the preposition carries it.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV 'his precious and exceeding great promises' keeps timia before megista, which excludes r01 (megista kai timia, 'exceeding great and precious'). It does not distinguish where hemin stands: 'he hath granted unto us' renders the pronoun the same whether it follows megista (base) or timia (r02). No note bears on the unit; the one note here is alternative_rendering.

The unit is the presence or absence of the article to with the following noun; English 'the corruption that is in the world by lust' would read identically either way, and Greek anarthrous nouns of this kind are regularly rendered definite. No mapped textual note; the single note is alternative_rendering and cannot decide a reading.

alignments.note: The ASV opens with the emphatic Yea, and; taking Yea for the postpositive de and and for kai. The reverse assignment is defensible.

No Greek preposition stands here, so the supplied frame for ... cause rides with the demonstrative under rule 67's noun-carrier arm, headed on the demonstrative's own word this rather than on the supplied cause. Rule 45's dia touto is the contrast, where an expressed preposition carries the frame.
The intensive pronoun is realized by very.

Rule 66: the head is the word glossing the compound's own base element, phil-, which *kindness* realizes, and not the modifier element adelph-. English word order does not decide it: 1PE.1.22 renders the same lexeme *love of the brethren* and heads on *love*, the same element, as TIT.3.4's philanthropia -> *love toward man* does.
Rule 20: the supplied possessive has no other source word to belong to, so it is the article's.

variant_decisions.evidence: hamartematon and hamartion are synonyms both rendered 'sins'; ASV 'the cleansing from his old sins' is the same English for either. The only note is alternative_rendering ('Or, closing his eyes') and concerns a different word.

Rule 33: the emphatic negation is one unit taking the whole English negation, here compressed into the single word 'never'. Rule 48's pattern, extended from eis ton aiona to a temporal particle, as JHN.6.35 does for ou me ... popote -> 'shall never thirst'. Reading the '-ever' of 'never' as answering to pote under rules 39 and 50 remains defensible, but rule 48 forecloses that same argument for aiona, which the corpus renders 'ever' elsewhere.
Rule 9: subject and auxiliary ride with the verb, headed on the lexical verb.

'never' answers to the negation whole and nothing is left over for the temporal particle, as at JHN.6.35 (popote). Where the ASV instead writes a separate 'ever' the particle is aligned, as at 2PE.1.21 and EPH.5.29. A reference comparison reports this token as a disagreement, and that report is not a correction (rule 48).
Auxiliaries ride with the lexical verb under rules 9 and 17.
The dative case preposition rides with the pronoun under rule 21.
Rule 20: the genitive pronoun displaces the article's determiner into our.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV 'I shall be ready always to put you in remembrance' renders the future mello ('I shall be about/ready to'). The rival ouk amelesa/ouk ameleso is a litotes, 'I will not be negligent to put you in remembrance'; the ASV shows no negative and no verb of negligence, so it renders the base.

alignments.note: Inflected verb takes its supplied subject and the anticipatory object pronoun as helpers; head on the lexical verb per rule 17.

The correlative frame *as ... as* answers to hoson alone and *long* to its quantity, so the preposition of the duration idiom has no separate English realization (rule 36). GAL.4.1's identical eph' hoson chronon leaves it unrepresented for the same reason, as does epi stadious at REV.21.16.

The discontinuous correlative frame is one unit under rule 15, headed on the quantity word as at JHN.6.11 *as much as* and GAL.4.1 *so ... as*; the corpus never splits an *as ... as* frame across two source units. With no chronon present, *long* has no noun of time to answer to and belongs here; contrast GAL.4.1, where it does.
Supplied subject pronoun is a helper on the finite verb per rules 7 and 9.
The attributive demonstrative supplies the English determiner, so the article realizes nothing (rule 38).
Discontinuous under rule 15: the infinitival 'to' and the phrasal particle 'up' belong to the verb, and the intervening 'you' is the pronoun's own.
The ASV expands the noun into a verbal phrase; head on 'remembrance', the token realizing the lexeme (rule 17).
Predicate adjective rendered adverbially with the supplied verb of motion.

Rule 82: where no correlative 'so' competes, a bare 'even' answers to kai, so kathos keeps only 'as'; 'even as' whole on kathos remains defensible.
Intensifying kai realized by 'even' (rules 65, 82).
Rule 20: the genitive hemon takes the possessive 'our', displacing the article.
Case preposition 'unto' rides with the dative pronoun (rules 21, 36).

Rule 17 heads the support-verb rendering on the meaning-bearing complement *diligence*. The supplied complementizer introduces the infinitive's own English clause and is its helper, not this verb's (rules 7, 40, 61), as PHP.4.14, TIT.1.16, 2CO.10.7, 2CO.11.5 and EPH.4.17 place it; rule 74's closing aside rests on JHN.5.39 alone, which is itself medium and concedes the infinitive.
Intensifying kai; the ASV writes no word for it (rule 65).
One Greek adverb rendered by a phrase; 'time' glosses the temporal element of hekastote, so rule 66 heads there, though 'every' remains defensible.

The infinitive is rendered as a finite clause and the supplied complementizer is its helper, discontinuously under rule 15 across the adverbial phrase and the expressed accusative subject, which aligns separately (rules 7, 40). Rule 17 heads on the lexical *able* rather than the modal or copula. As at 2PE.1.19, where the participle likewise carries its own *that*.
The first-person possessive adjective carries 'my', so the article realizes nothing (rules 54, 20).
Infinitival 'to' is the verb's own helper, no conjunction governing the clause (rules 7, 40).
Article governing mnemen across the interposed genitive (rule 57); the ASV supplies no determiner, so it realizes nothing (rule 23).
Rule 17 heads the substantival demonstrative on 'these', the supplied 'things' completing it.
The ASV spells both elements of the light-verb pair out, so it splits under rule 2; 'to' is the noun's case helper.
ASV renders the aorist participle as the main clause verb; supplied subject and auxiliary ride with it under rules 7 and 9, headed on the lexical verb.

Rule 9: the supplied subject and the auxiliary-like *made* ride with the inflected verb, headed on the lexical *known* under rule 17. The supplied subordinator *when* is a separate `added` unit: no Greek conjunction stands in this verse for rule 40 to realize, and the corpus puts a supplied *when* on a participle in 66 of 67 units and on no finite indicative.

Rule 5: the ASV subordinates this clause to the preceding one, but no source token licenses *when*. Rule 40 realizes an expressed Greek conjunction and there is none here; the subordination the ASV inverts belongs to the participle exakolouthesantes, which has already spent its English on the main clause *we did follow*. As PHP.1.22 and PHP.1.20, where a supplied subordinator with no local licensor is `added`.
The supplied possessive *our* belongs to the genitive pronoun, so the article is displaced under rule 20 and the case preposition *of* stays with the noun.
Discontinuous under rule 15; *of* is the case preposition riding with the noun.
The Greek expresses the verb, so *we were* is its own; the predicate noun stands alone.
The demonstrative occupies the English determiner slot with *his*, so the article realizes nothing under rules 20 and 38.
Discontinuous under rule 15; *of* is the case preposition riding with the noun.
Supplied subject of the participle is a rule 7/9 helper; head on the lexical verb.

Genitive absolute rendered as a finite clause; the subordinator, expletive subject and copula are helpers on the participle under rules 7 and 9.
Anarthrous Greek: the supplied indefinite is a rule 51 helper on the noun.

variant_decisions.evidence: ASV 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased' is the fixed English order for this saying and does not report where houtos estin stood in the Greek; nor does collapsing 'my Son, my beloved' into 'my beloved Son' reveal whether the second mou was present. The only note is a greek_gloss on 'having received'.

variant_decisions.evidence: Both readings say 'in the holy mount'; the difference is attributive order and the extra article (hagio orei vs orei to hagio), which English cannot show. No note is attached to the verse.

alignments.note: Inflected verb takes its English subject; head on the lexical verb per rule 9.
ASV renders the adjective by 'of prophecy'; the supplied 'of' belongs to that phrase rather than to the accusative noun. Head on the lexical noun per rule 17.
The italicized 'made' is the supplied verb of the resultative predicate the comparative adjective heads (rules 11, 53); head on 'sure' per rule 17.
Portmanteau: '-unto' realizes the dative case of the relative (rule 35).

The participle is rendered as a finite clause; the supplied complementizer is its helper under rules 7 and 40 and the supplied subject under rule 9. Not rule 31, which is scoped to an attributive participle governed by an article and to a supplied relativizer; prosechontes is anarthrous and supplementary. *take heed* is a support-verb rendering, so the head is the meaning-bearing complement (rule 17). PHP.4.14's kalos epoiesate plus participle is the same idiom and is analysed the same way.
'unto' realizes the dative case and the supplied 'a' determines the anarthrous noun (rules 21, 51).
Both adjective and noun are anarthrous, so the supplied determiner belongs to the noun (rule 58); discontinuous under rule 15.
In 'until' the ASV realizes the adverb alone; the genitive relative of the idiom has no English word of its own (rule 23). A reference comparison may report this as a disagreement.
Anarthrous noun with a supplied determiner (rule 51).

One Greek word rendered by the compound *day star* with a supplied determiner (rules 51, 58). The -phoros element has no English word, so the archiereus/zoon class does not reach this; *star* glosses the lexeme's substantival denotation while *day* answers phos-, and the corpus anchors *star* to aster in 16 units. Heading on *day* remains defensible, as at praitorion PHP.1.13 and prothesmia GAL.4.2.
The genitive pronoun takes the possessive, so the article is displaced (rule 20).
Reported speech with an expressed complementizer, so the conjunction aligns to that; not the recitative case of rule 43.

The ASV writes the negation once, as *no*, and leaves pasa no separate English word, so rule 39's test joins the pair into one discontinuous unit under rule 15. Rules 41 and 59 do not empty the negator, pas being no negative, but those settle emptying and not joining; rule 80 is a different construction, a quantifier with a substantival article that rule 32 can empty. As 1JN.2.21, 1JN.3.15, EPH.5.5, GAL.2.16 and REV.22.3, all of them medium. Giving *no* to ou alone and leaving pasa unrepresented remains defensible.
Anarthrous genitive rendered 'of + noun'; the case preposition rides with the noun under rules 21 and 17.
Discontinuous under rule 15: the case preposition 'of' belongs to the governed noun, the attributive adjective standing between them.
The ASV renders this instance of the adjective as plain 'private' rather than a possessive, so rule 47's displacement is not in question.
The clause negation is realized in the determiner 'no'.
Anarthrous dative; the supplied 'by the' rides with the noun under rules 21 and 58.
Case preposition 'of' rides with the noun.
Auxiliary 'being' is the participle's helper; head on the lexical verb.
Both adjective and noun are anarthrous, so the supplied determiner belongs to the noun under rule 58.

variant_decisions.evidence: The unit is only the order of prophecy and pote; ASV 'For no prophecy ever came by the will of man' renders either arrangement identically. The verse's single note is a greek_gloss on 'was brought'.

ASV reads 'but men spake from God': 'from God' renders the preposition apo with theou, the base reading. The rival substitutes hagioi, yielding 'holy men of God spake'; the ASV has no 'holy' with 'men' here, reserving 'Holy' for the Spirit, so it renders the base.
